title: Trump to Canadian plane maker Bombardier: You can't sell in U.S. unless you build in U.S.
sourceDescription: U.S. President Donald Trump says Bombardier would no longer be allowed to sell in the U.S. unless ​the Montreal-based airplane company starts manufacturing in the states.
sourceBodyText:

Bombardier is the target of Donald Trump's latest salvo amid the U.S.-Canada trade war, with the U.S. president threatening to block its plane sales in the U.S. if it doesn't shift manufacturing stateside. File photo shows jet planes being built at Bombardier's aircraft assembly centre in Mississauga, Ont., on May 8. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press) Social Sharing U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that Montreal-based airplane maker Bombardier would no longer be allowed to sell in the United States unless ​it starts manufacturing in the states.

"NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER ​IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!" Trump said in Truth Social post.

"If they want our Market, they must ​build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank.'"

Trump's post, ⁠which comes amid a ⁠growing trade dispute between Washington and Ottawa, ‌was the latest salvo in his campaign to pressure foreign and domestic companies to manufacture more products in the U.S.

No talks scheduled as Canada's counter-tariffs against U.S. set to take effect at 12:01 a.m.

That objective has driven many economic policies in his second term, especially a near global tariff wall that ⁠has drawn complaints from many U.S. trading partners.

Canada is set to introduce a wave of counter-tariffs against the United States early Tuesday.

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette said on social media on Monday that she won't respond to Trump's provocations with more provocations.

"Bombardier is a source of pride for Quebec, a flagship of our economy, and a major player in our aerospace industry. Behind this company are thousands of Quebec workers who showcase our expertise around the world," she wrote in French.

"I have reached out to Eric Martel, CEO of Bombardier, to offer him our full support."

Trump tells Bombardier it can't sell in the U.S. unless it builds in the U.S.

September 7 | Duration 5:12 U.S. President Donald Trump said in a social media post Monday that Montreal-based jet maker Bombardier would no longer be allowed to sell in the United States unless it started manufacturing there, even though the company does have a manufacturing footprint in the country. The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on how Trump would enforce the action targeting Bombardier or the steps ‌he would take to bar deliveries of Bombardier jets that have been approved by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

The company's jets also comply with the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) trade deal that Trump helped implement.

Bombardier issued a statement late Monday highlighting the work it already does in the U.S., as well as plans for expansion, saying its aircraft create "tens of thousands of U.S. jobs."

"Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its U.S. employees. Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers and the communities in which we operate across the country," the statement said.

U.S. aerospace analyst Richard Aboulafia said he didn't believe any business jet customers ⁠would cancel Bombardier orders and didn't see how Trump could stop them from being sold.

Aboulafia said most Bombardier private jets use U.S. engines, which are produced by Honeywell Aerospace and GE Aerospace.

Aerospace has largely emerged unscathed from the tariff war, with ‌the flow of parts and planes not currently impacted by duties. According to U.S. trade group Aerospace Industries Association, the country's aerospace and defence sector has a $109.2 billion US trade surplus, with exports up 25 per cent on an annual basis in 2025.

Donald Trump mistakes Bank of Canada for retail bank

A Michigan Democrat wants to put Canada on the ballot during the midterms. Are voters listening?

Like the U.S. auto sector, which depends on Canadian parts production, aerospace is ​highly integrated on a global scale.

Bombardier, the rival of U.S. business jet manufacturer Gulfstream Aerospace, has an American workforce of 3,500 and a U.S. footprint of 2,800 suppliers, along ⁠with factories and service centres in the country. The company is now adding its sixth U.S. service centre and ⁠produces wings for its flagship Global 8000 jet in Texas.

Bombardier also has a defence division with a U.S.-based factory, in Kansas, where it prepares planes for special mission purposes. About half of the fleet of 5,100 aircraft operated by Bombardier customers are located in the U.S.

Trump trying to destroy Canada’s manufacturing base: Unifor president

August 22 | Duration 1:30 Amid the aftermath of last-minute trade talks breaking down, Unifor national president Lana Payne says the Trump administration is purposely targeting Canada’s manufacturing sector. In January, Trump said the U.S. was decertifying Bombardier Global Express ⁠business jets and threatened 50 per cent import tariffs on all aircraft made in Canada ⁠until the country's regulator certified a number of planes produced by U.S. rival Gulfstream. Neither ⁠occurred, ⁠but the following month, Canada ​certified several Gulfstream planes.

Bombardier announced on Sept. 1 that it would acquire a Canadian factory ​from supplier Mitsubishi Heavy ⁠Industries, which manufactures wings for the private jet maker's Global 5500 and 6500 aircraft.

In July, Bombardier reported that its quarterly revenue grew six per cent compared with the same three months a year ago to $2.15 billion U.S., helped by strong demand for aftermarket services.

John Gradek, a faculty lecturer in supply chain networks and aviation management at Montreal's McGill University, says he's not sure Trump has put "a lot of thought" into what barring Bombardier planes would mean for U.S. citizens and the company's U.S. employees.

Nonetheless, he suspects Trump will turn his attention to other Canadian companies as the trade dispute continues, saying the plane maker will be the "first of many" targets.

Trump says not doing business with Canada is an option

"He's taking a shot at a company that has been very successful in attracting U.S. buyers, and he thinks by doing that, he will in fact spread ruin on the Canadian economy," Gradek said, adding that he hopes Canada considers retaliatory action.

"There are many other very successful Canadian companies operating in the U.S. I'm not sure who the next target will be, but there will be others."

title: Repair begins on damage from devastating storm, washing over Cape Breton
sourceDescription: Holes on the road created by the washouts could be several feet deep and eight to 10 feet long, Inverness County councillor says
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Repair begins on damage from devastating storm, washing over Cape Breton Om Shanbhag Published 15 hours ago Open this photo in gallery: An onlooker makes images from a bridge over the flooded River Tillard, in Richmond County, Cape Breton, N.S., on Saturday. Steve Wadden/The Canadian Press

Heavy rain fell on parts of Nova Scotia on Monday as the province began to repair the damage left by a slow-moving storm that passed over Cape Breton Island, washing out roads, leaving thousands without power and one person dead.

Early Monday morning, Environment and Climate Change Canada issued a hazardous weather alert forecasting up to 25 to 40 millimetres of heavy rain, after 200 millimetres fell on the island and parts of the northern mainland over less than two days.

The ground could not absorb more rainfall and water would likely pool on roads and low-lying areas, the weather service warned. The alert ended in the afternoon on Monday.

“It just poured and poured, and then we had a lot of wind. It wasn’t a hurricane, but it wasn’t too far from it,” said Inverness County councillor John MacLennan. On Sunday, he left his home near Whycocomagh, N.S., to inspect the damage done by the storm.

Some roads nearby had two or three washouts, Mr. MacLennan said, on gravel and paved roads alike. He said the holes created by the washouts could be several feet deep and eight to 10 feet long.

“The rain, when it started late in the evening, it never stopped, and we had a lot of flooded roads. Roads wiped out. Culverts wiped out,” Mr. MacLellan said.

He said some of his constituents faced severe damage to their homes owing to flooding from the storm. A neighbour visiting their daughter in Alberta asked him to check up on their home.

Mr. MacLennan said he was met with four feet of water inside the house, a toppled water heater and cupboards pulled away from the wall. The stove had a fine layer of silt on it, hinting that the water level had previously been higher.

In hard-hit Richmond County, Scott Touesnard, who owns a dock-building company, said the biggest change since the storm has been the loss of a train trestle he used to sit on as a child.

“The train had stopped going there years and years ago. But half of that is washed in the water, and then the water washed behind it as well, and took out a big part of the land,” he said.

One dead after Cape Breton floods prompt state of emergency, cut power for thousands

Mr. Touesnard said there are some washouts near his business, but that it hasn’t stopped him from being able to get around.

A 46-year-old woman from Richmond County was found dead Saturday several hours after her abandoned vehicle was discovered near a flooded bridge. RCMP said Sunday the death is not believed to be suspicious and added they would not provide any more information.

On Saturday, Nova Scotia Power said in an online post that restoration of power may be delayed by washed-out roads. By Monday, all large-scale power outages in the area were resolved, though smaller outages persisted.

Lois Landry, warden of Richmond County, said a Zodiac rescue boat operated by a local fire department and a provincial helicopter were used to carry out daily wellness checks for any residents completely cut off by flooding.

Guests stranded at the Lakeside Luxury Domes camp in the Saint George’s Channel area created a makeshift, jerry-rigged exit route after the property was washed out, she said.

“We’re used to hurricanes on the East Coast, that’s not new to us. But there was wind coupled with rain we haven’t seen the likes of, really, ever,” she said.

Fred Tilley, Nova Scotia Minister of Public Works, said hundreds of provincial employees and local contractors are working to restore the entirety of Cape Breton Island’s road network within the coming days.

“It’s another one of these one-in-100-years storms that has wreaked havoc,” he said. “It’s always top of mind when we’re rebuilding to build for climate change where possible.”

While the province prepared for the storm, Mr. Tilley said, “there’s not much infrastructure that can handle that in Nova Scotia.”

At the peak of the flooding, according to a spokesperson for the province’s Department of Public Works, there were more than 120 closed or damaged roads on Cape Breton.

“Currently, about 44 are closed. The rest have either fully or partially reopened, including dozens overnight,” Toby Koffman, communications director for the department, said in a statement Monday.

Mr. Koffman said that two of eight bridges that were damaged will need to be replaced. As well, he said there are more than 200 culverts that were washed away, from driveways to major roads.

Ms. Landry said she’s lived on Cape Breton Island all of her 58 years, but she’s never seen so much flooding before.

A rainfall device in the area of Saint George’s Channel measured 230 millimetres of rain before it broke, she added.

“We really can’t even wrap our heads around that much rain … it compromised the ground beneath our infrastructure.”
